toc.title: Applying this to a possible new narrative

blocks.p: This part is nerdy, but I promise it will be painless.

Your Autonomic Nervous System (ANS) governs all your internal organs and processes without conscious direction or effort. It's involuntary and automatic. Breathing, heart rate, sweating, pupil dilation, internal temperature regulation, digestion, and more are not functions you must direct or plan out. If they were, daily living would probably be a lot more difficult.

Imagine having to be aware of and control your heartbeat. Or your breathing. Or your digestion. Now, imagine doing all of these things at the same time. Now imagine doing all of these things at the same time while also knowing the optimal levels of each. And even if you could do all of that, could you also adjust to what is necessary to the specific environment in that particular moment, then adjust to the next environment in the next moment? Probably not.

But that's what your ANS does. It optimizes your body's resources and functions based on the context of the situation. It will adjust your pupil dilation based on the area's light. It'll regulate your breathing based on your body's current oxygen demands.

Your ANS also adjusts to varying levels of safety, danger, or life threat every moment of every day. It shifts all bodily functions based on what's necessary for survival. Even now, your wonderful ANS is scanning for safety or danger through your senses. It does all of this passively, in the background, without your awareness.

If we could pull off all of that on a conscious level, we probably wouldn't also enjoy a Netflix binge simultaneously. You couldn't read this. We have a hard enough time just focusing on the person in front of us and sustaining a conversation! It's a good thing, then, that the ANS is outside of our conscious control.

The ANS is historically and generally known as two antagonistic systems, sympathetic and parasympathetic, as if these two were competing against each other for dominance. However, Dr. Stephen Porges explains that it's more complex in his Polyvagal Theory. The theory hypothesizes that one sympathetic system and two parasympathetic systems work together to benefit the mammalian organism. They are not antagonistic but complement each other and serve different functions based on the moment's needs.

The sympathetic system, located in the spinal cord, is the biological pathway for the flight/fight response. The flight/fight mobilization system is ideal for attacking a threat or fleeing to safety. If you notice your flight/fight system activate, you will likely notice shorter breaths, increased heart rate, and muscle tension.

The two parasympathetic systems both utilize the vagus nerve (*poly*vagal, though *bi*vagal may have been better?). The first and oldest parasympathetic system is the immobility system, which is associated with the dorsal vagal part of the brainstem and extends to the gut. This system is responsible for collapsing in life-threatening situations. The second parasympathetic system is the social engagement system, which extends from the brainstem, connecting the face, neck, and heart. This system becomes active when an individual is in a safe environment, facilitating social connection with other safe mammals.

The autonomic nervous system shifts amongst these three bodily states, repurposing internal organs and processes for the demands of the moment, either prosocial or defensive. For example, when in danger and more sympathetically charged, the mouth may go dry. The body no longer needs saliva to help chew food: it's now mobilized for running or fighting. The ANS prioritizes bodily processes based on what it detects as safe, dangerous, or life-threatening. When under life threat, all systems are reduced to support basic life maintenance, such as heart rate and breathing. The entire body slows down, imitating a corpse.

The point is that the ANS is always working and doing so outside of our conscious control. It allows you to survive and maintain a basic level of functioning so that you can then direct your conscious attention elsewhere.
Our autonomic nervous system is basically in one of three different states. These are the primary states of the ANS:
There are also mixed states, which are combinations of the primary states:

These primary and mixed states each evolved within us to enhance survival chances and optimize bodily functions and resources. They benefit us and other organisms by increasing the chances of passing genetic code.

It's important to recognize these different states and what they look and feel like. Each has its own experience, and differentiating amongst them can make your internal experiences more manageable, at least cognitively. We'll spend a lot of time understanding these primary and mixed states in depth. But before that, we need to learn how they interact with each other and how the ANS utilizes each state.

The Polyvagal Ladder is a metaphor from Deb Dana that helps us understand how we move through our primary autonomic states. Just like with a ladder, our active autonomic state shifts up and down in order, sequentially. The active state does not skip rungs of the ladder; it moves through them one by one.

Also, like a ladder, there's a top, middle, and bottom to our primary Polyvagal states. Quite literally. The safety pathways (ventral vagal) connect our brainstem to our heart, neck, and facial muscles. The safety state is the highest point of the Polyvagal ladder and is at the top of our bodies. In the middle rung of the Polyvagal ladder is the flight/fight system (sympathetic), which is in the spinal cord and chest. At the bottom of the ladder is the shutdown system (dorsal vagal), residing in the gut.

If you aren't literally safe, you lose access to the safety pathways and drop down your ladder into the flight/fight system. The first sympathetic impulse is to escape danger, create space, and get to safety. But if that doesn't work, the second sympathetic impulse is to use aggression, closing space to get the danger to back off. If aggression doesn't work, you drop down further into your shutdown system and collapse in immobilization. This is a sequence of shifts, not a choice you make. Like a ladder, you climb down and climb up in a sequence. Same with our autonomic states: we shift through them in a sequence. Not as a result of choice.

The reverse is also true. If you exist in a shutdown state, you need to climb your Polyvagal ladder through flight/fight and back into safety. You don't skip flight/fight from shutdown and enter your safety state.
Let's illustrate the Polyvagal ladder metaphor through two scenarios. The first is a more obvious one, focusing on actual survival. The second is a human example not directly related to survival.
Imagine a herd of gazelles on the open plain, grazing and chatting with each other about recent herd events. They feel relaxed and connected in their safety states.

They hear something moving in the brush and turn their heads in the direction of the sound. One of them says, "Did everyone else hear that?" They nod; they did indeed hear it. "Okay, here's what we're going t-"
Suddenly, a lion springs out of the brush, sprinting toward the herd. The herd members each drop out of their safety state, into their sympathetic flight/fight state and run as fast as possible.

But the lion catches one of them, pouncing and dragging it to the ground. Its flight activation was insufficient, and it could not act on any aggressive fight impulse it may have. The gazelle collapses limply into its shutdown state: not dead but immobile.

The lion pauses to breathe, panting in recovery from using its sympathetic energy. Its enormous body desperately needs oxygen. A pack of hyenas approaches the scene, opportunistically seeking out the "kill." The lion growls, "Back off before I make you back off," to the hyena pack. And they respond, "You and what army?" The lion is stumped; its brain freezes with no response.

Our gazelle friend unconsciously detects an opportunity to escape! It uses its power and sympathetic fight state to push off the ground and swing its majestic gazelle head around, creating space. Then, as the hyenas and lion reel back, the gazelle sprints for safety using its flight activation.

It reaches its herd, and they greet it with whatever greeting gazelles do, each re-accessing its safety state. Indeed, a beautiful sight, surely. I assume. I really don't know, but you get the idea. Look, it's just a made-up example to illustrate the Polyvagal ladder. And it's entertaining, too.

Imagine you're at work, feeling relaxed and engaged with your colleagues (I said "imagine" for a reason!). You're in your safety state, at the top of your Polyvagal ladder. You're collaboratively working, sharing ideas, smiling, and everyone is enthralled with you and everything about you.

Suddenly, you're informed that you must give an impromptu presentation to the entire team, including higher-ups, in just a few minutes. Not only that but your job and livelihood depend on your success! Your state quickly shifts to flight activation. "Oh, crud!" you exclaim to yourself (but also loud enough for others to hear). Your heart rate increases, your palms get sweaty, and your mind races as you desperately attempt to think of a way out of the situation. But there is none.

You get angry, entering your fight state. "How dare they do this to me! How dare they bombard me with this unlikely and happenstance situation! This is an outrage of the highest order!" You say these words in your mind, keeping your fight energy inside. It would be inappropriate to say aloud and likely result in your termination from your position and the adoration of your colleagues. You clench your fist and march forward into the conference room.

As you begin the presentation, you start to feel overwhelmed by the staring eyes and the importance of the moment. You find it hard to focus, and your voice falters. You think about losing your job, being "booed" by your colleagues, and tomatoes being chucked your way. You've entered the shutdown state, feeling disconnection and numbness, but somehow make it through the presentation, seemingly on autopilot.
After the presentation is over, you receive some positive feedback. Your colleagues say, "We had no idea you knew so much about [whatever thing]! Great job, colleague!"
"Really?" you say nervously, looking at the ground. Your eyes dart up at them briefly. "You really mean that?"
"Indeed we do," they each say simultaneously.
"I was so upset! Wow, what a relief!" Energy comes back into your system as you laugh nervously with an awkward smile, feeling on edge and unsure if you trust the feedback.
"No, we really mean it. You have incredibly extensive knowledge of [whatever thing] and present it very well. Great job!"
You smile, take a deep breath, and exhale slowly, relaxing into your safety state. "Hey, let's all spend time together doing something social and smiling."
And so you do.

Remember: these states are functions of the autonomic nervous system (ANS). These autonomic shifts operate largely outside of our conscious awareness and control. The ANS constantly regulates vital functions like heart rate, digestion, respiratory rate, and more. In response to our environment, the ANS seamlessly shifts between states of safety, mobilization, and immobilization. But it does so sequentially, not randomly.

These shifts are not choices we make; they are autonomic responses that evolved to enhance the potential of survival. The ANS adapts to perceived threats or safety cues by transitioning through different physiological states. This process occurs without our conscious input, which means we don't get to choose the autonomic state we find ourselves in at any given moment.

Our capacity for social engagement, or lack thereof, is inherently tied to autonomic functioning. The same applies to other reactions, like running, fighting, collapsing, appeasing, or freezing. Shifting into and out of these states is a dynamic, fluid process.

Understanding the lack of conscious control over these shifts is important, and I can't stress this enough. This is foundational in creating a new narrative for yourself: autonomic states are not under your conscious control! You can't choose to switch states. Our reactions to stress or traumatic incidents are not a matter of choice or character but rather the result of deeply ingrained biological processes (and a healthy dose of nurture along with the nature).

However, these autonomic responses can become dysregulated. One can actually get stuck in a defensive state, making movement through the Polyvagal ladder much more difficult, including accessing the safety state.

There are some pieces of good news: (1) even though you can't consciously control and change your autonomic state, you can consciously set yourself up for a greater likelihood of shifting up your Polyvagal ladder. (2) You can also consciously experience your states as they are and as they shift. (3) You can consciously feel and experience more safety in your body, then extend it further. (4) You can consciously reduce obstacles to Polyvagal ladder climbing.

blocks.why: You can't choose your state, but you can set yourself up to climb. This practice is one way to do that.

blocks.h: Applying this to a possible new narrative

blocks.p: When we look back at things we've been through, we often blame ourselves for how we did or did not react. Like, "I should have _" or "If only I didn't ___." But again, our Polyvagal states are not an issue of choice. Neither are the behaviors we have access to from our state. Ladder climbing is a sequence of events, not a menu of options. No one is picking their autonomic state or how they react to traumatic situations.

As I share this basic level of Polyvagal Theory knowledge with my therapy clients, I often see a gloss come over their faces. Their affect goes flat, but not in a disconnected way. Their minds go to some memory, and they rapidly piece together a new understanding of what they went through. Instead of blame, there is now an opening for understanding and self-compassion.
I hope you build that for yourself as well. I invite you to objectively look at what you have learned so far and apply it to yourself as best you can. Objectivity with ourselves is not easy.

For now, focus on the teachings I've covered so far: autonomic states, unconscious autonomic shifts, and the body's preparation for safety or defense based on the context of the situation. With these few pieces in mind, answer these next journaling prompts when ready. Keep it light. Don't journal about specific traumatic incidents and their details. It's enough to recognize the past event for now without reliving it. If this is too much for you, continue reading and come back to this when you are ready.

blocks.prompt: Is there a past situation for which you blame or judge yourself? Do you wish you had done something or not done something? (A simple "yes" or "no" is sufficient for now.)
Is it possible that you experienced an autonomic shift that was out of your control? Is it possible that you did not choose your behavioral response? (A simple "yes" or "no" is sufficient for now.)

If it's true that your body shifted to a defensive state, how does that impact your view of this situation? How does that impact your view of yourself in that moment? How about your view of yourself now?

q: "Polyvagal Theory uses an inclusive definition of the autonomic nervous system that includes sensory pathways and emphasizes the brain stem areas regulating autonomic function... In contrast to the traditional model that focuses on tonic motor influences on visceral organs, Polyvagal Theory emphasizes autonomic reactivity... [and] proposes a phylogenetically ordered hierarchy in which autonomic subsystems react to challenges in the reverse of their evolutionary history, consistent with the principle of dissolution." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W. (2018). Polyvagal theory: A primer. In S. W. Porges & D. Dana (Eds.), Clinical Applications of the Polyvagal Theory: The Emergence of Polyvagal-Informed Therapies (pp. 50–61). W. W. Norton & Company.

blocks.p: My translation: We react to danger in a specific order: safety, then flight/fight, then shutdown. "Dissolution" helps explain this sequence. Also, the brainstem is super important.

q: "The vagus nerve is a conduit. It's a wire. That's not really what we're concerned about. We're concerned about the regulator that's sending signals through that wire and the impact of those signals to the target organs. And then the target organs... sending signals back to the brain. We're more concerned with the feedback loop between organ and brainstem that's going through the vagus than the nerve itself." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Sunseri, J. (Host). (2019). Dr. Stephen Porges interview: Mental disorders, substance use, psychiatry & the polyvagal theory (Episode 15). In Stuck Not Broken [Podcast].

blocks.p: My translation: Stop focusing on the vagus nerve. Instead, focus on the information sent through it from brain to body and body to brain.
